column1: What fatal flaw plagued the 1949 'Automatic Binding Bricks' design, and why did it fail structurally?
column2: The hollow rectangular bricks had studs on top but an empty interior cavity, relying only on friction between studs and the walls of the brick below. This gave insufficient clutch power, causing structures to collapse under lateral shear or when lifted.

column1: What geometric innovation did Godtfred Kirk Christiansen introduce in 1958, and what mechanism did it create?
column2: Cylindrical tubes molded into the underside of each brick, positioned concentrically beneath alternating studs, creating a three-dimensional interference fit with elastic deformation ('frictional engagement with automatic and elastic return').

column1: What was the founding invariant of the Lego System formalized by Godtfred Kirk Christiansen in the 1950s?
column2: That every element, regardless of which set it originated from, must interlock constructively with every other element ever produced — a system of combinatorial, narrative-agnostic openness.

column1: How did the 1998 Lucasfilm licensing deal invert Lego's traditional product architecture?
column2: It shifted the system from material-first (narrative-agnostic, generic parts) to narrative-first: sets became purposeful assemblages of newly designed, often exclusively printed or colored elements locked into representing a specific fictional outcome.

column1: Before the licensing era, under what condition did new Lego elements enter the parts catalog?
column2: Only when existing elements could not accomplish a required mechanical or representational function — growth was governed by structural necessity, not marketing or film art direction.

column1: What cost pressures did Lego's licensing-driven parts expansion introduce after 1999?
column2: New mold tooling ($50,000–$300,000 per element), new color-matched ABS formulations, and new printing pad setups, all needing recovery through set sales that also bore royalty payments to external rights holders.

column1: What was Lego's 'open-loop' limitation prior to Mindstorms, even with Technic sets?
column2: Every motion was a direct consequence of a human hand applying force — there was no feedback, memory, or behavior; the model did nothing unless physically moved by the child.

column1: Define the 'embodied computation principle' that persisted from the RCX through the EV3.
column2: The program is inseparable from the physical structure hosting it — a given piece of code (e.g., a PID loop) describes how a specific chassis geometry, sensor placement, and motor dynamics interact with a specific environment; changing the physical build breaks the program's validity.

column1: What microcontroller powered the original Mindstorms RCX, and what two capabilities did it bring to a plastic brick for the first time?
column2: A 32-bit Renesas H8/3292 microcontroller, bringing infrared communication and a visual programming environment into the brick system — i.e., closed-loop computation.

column1: What three monomers compose ABS, and what mechanical property does each primarily contribute to Lego bricks?
column2: Acrylonitrile: chemical resistance and thermal stability (raises glass transition temp to ~105°C). Butadiene: impact resistance via dispersed elastomeric particles (prevents brittle failure). Styrene: processability and surface gloss (controls melt flow for injection molding).

column1: What dimensional tolerance has Lego maintained since 1963's shift to ABS, and why is it significant?
column2: A tolerance of approximately ten micrometers, ensuring bricks molded decades and continents apart (e.g., Denmark 1975 vs. Mexico 2024) remain perfectly interchangeable — the basis of infinite compatibility.

column1: In clutch power testing, how much does pull force (in Newtons) decrease per 10°C rise above 20°C, and what causes this?
column2: Clutch power decreases 0.3N per 10°C above 20°C, due to thermal expansion of the ABS plastic reducing the interference fit.
